claim: Synthesis of 5-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) is the rate-limiting step in tetrapyrrole biosynthesis in land plants.
source: Synthesis of 5-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) is the rate-limiting step in tetrapyrrole biosynthesis in land plants.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental support in this manuscript.

claim: In photosynthetic eukaryotes and many bacteria, glutamyl-tRNA reductase (GluTR) is the most tightly controlled enzyme upstream of ALA.
source: In photosynthetic eukaryotes and many bacteria, glutamyl-tRNA reductase (GluTR) is the most tightly controlled enzyme upstream of ALA.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Higher plants possess two GluTR isoforms: GluTR1 is predominantly expressed in green tissue, and GluTR2 is constitutively expressed in all organs.
source: Higher plants possess two GluTR isoforms: GluTR1 is predominantly expressed in green tissue, and GluTR2 is constitutively expressed in all organs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Accumulation of heme, induced by feeding with ALA, stimulates Clp-protease-dependent degradation of Arabidopsis GluTR1.
source: Here, we report that accumulation of heme, induced by feeding with ALA, stimulates Clp-protease-dependent degradation of Arabidopsis GluTR1.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1-5.

claim: Binding of heme to the GluTR-binding protein (GBP) inhibits interaction of GBP with the N-terminal regulatory domain of GluTR1.
source: We demonstrate that binding of heme to the GluTR-binding protein (GBP) inhibits interaction of GBP with the N-terminal regulatory domain of GluTR1, thus making it accessible to the Clp protease.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Binding of heme to GBP makes GluTR1 accessible to the Clp protease.
source: We demonstrate that binding of heme to the GluTR-binding protein (GBP) inhibits interaction of GBP with the N-terminal regulatory domain of GluTR1, thus making it accessible to the Clp protease.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and the proposed model in Figure 8.

claim: The plastid-localized TBS is initiated by the reduction of a tRNA-coupled glutamate to glutamate-1-semialdehyde (GSA) by glutamyl-tRNA reductase (GluTR).
source: In plants, the plastid-localized TBS is initiated by the reduction of a tRNA-coupled glutamate to glutamate-1-semialdehyde (GSA) by glutamyl-tRNA reductase (GluTR).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The unstable GSA is converted into 5-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) by GSA aminotransferase (GSAT).
source: The unstable GSA is then converted into 5-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) by GSA aminotransferase (GSAT).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: ALA is the universal precursor of all tetrapyrroles.
source: ALA is the universal precursor of all tetrapyrroles, and its synthesis is considered to be rate-limiting for TBS as a whole.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: ALA synthesis is considered to be rate-limiting for TBS as a whole.
source: ALA is the universal precursor of all tetrapyrroles, and its synthesis is considered to be rate-limiting for TBS as a whole.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Eight molecules of ALA are converted into the macrocyclic protoporphyrin IX (ProtoIX) in subsequent reactions.
source: Eight molecules of ALA are converted into the macrocyclic protoporphyrin IX (ProtoIX) in subsequent reactions.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: ProtoIX is directed into either the iron or magnesium branch for the synthesis of heme or Chl, respectively.
source: Thereafter, ProtoIX is directed into either the iron or magnesium branch for the synthesis of heme or Chl, respectively (Tanaka and Tanaka, 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: For heme synthesis in plants, two related ferrochelatases (FC1 and FC2) are available, which are characterized by distinct and partially overlapping functions.
source: For heme synthesis in plants, two related ferrochelatases (FC1 and FC2) are available, which are characterized by distinct and partially overlapping functions (Espinas et al., 2016; Fan et al., 2019; Hey et al., 2016; Scharfenberg et al., 2015; Woodson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Synthesis of Chl is initiated by the insertion of Mg2+ into ProtoIX, catalyzed by the Mg-chelatase (MgCh) complex.
source: Synthesis of Chl is initiated by the insertion of Mg2+ into ProtoIX, catalyzed by the Mg-chelatase (MgCh) complex.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Binding of the N-terminus of Arabidopsis GluTR1 to ClpS, ClpF, and ClpC induces its proteolysis.
source: Binding of the N-terminus of Arabidopsis GluTR1 to ClpS, ClpF, and ClpC induces its proteolysis (Apitz et al., 2016; Nishimura et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Plant GBP competes with the Clp subunits for binding to the N-terminus of GluTR, and thus counteracts GluTR breakdown.
source: Plant GBP, which has no homolog in bacteria, competes with the Clp subunits for binding to the N-terminus of GluTR, and thus counteracts GluTR breakdown (Apitz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Deletion of the HBD was found to compromise heme-dependent inhibition of GluTR activity in vitro.
source: Deletion of the HBD was found to compromise heme-dependent inhibition of GluTR activity in vitro (Vothknecht et al., 1998) and Clp-dependent degradation of GluTR in plants (Apitz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Deletion of the HBD was found to compromise Clp-dependent degradation of GluTR in plants.
source: Deletion of the HBD was found to compromise heme-dependent inhibition of GluTR activity in vitro (Vothknecht et al., 1998) and Clp-dependent degradation of GluTR in plants (Apitz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: The N-terminus of GluTR – a putative heme-binding domain (HBD) – is not involved in heme binding.
source: The results presented in this study reveal that the N-terminus of GluTR – a putative heme-binding domain (HBD) – is not involved in heme binding.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The importance of heme for GluTR1 stability derives from its interaction with GBP.
source: The importance of heme for GluTR1 stability derives from its interaction with GBP.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: GluTR1 content decreased in control leaves in the dark.
source: Accumulation of FC1 was strongly induced, and GluTR1 content decreased in control leaves in the dark, but these effects became markedly more pronounced in the presence of supplied ALA.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: GluTR1 content decreased more markedly in the presence of supplied ALA.
source: Accumulation of FC1 was strongly induced, and GluTR1 content decreased in control leaves in the dark, but these effects became markedly more pronounced in the presence of supplied ALA.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: GluTR1 amounts were slightly reduced after 4 hr and reduced by 40% after 24 hr of darkness without ALA supply compared to light-grown seedlings at t(0).
source: In comparison to the light-grown seedlings at t(0), GluTR1 amounts were slightly reduced after 4 hr and reduced by 40% after 24 hr of darkness without ALA supply.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Short term (4 hr) ALA feeding triggered a drastic loss of GluTR1 (76% reduction relative to t(0)).
source: But even short term (4 hr) ALA feeding triggered a drastic loss of GluTR1 (76% reduction relative to t(0)), while the enzyme was barely detectable after 24 hr of ALA treatment (96% reduction relative to t(0), Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: GluTR1 was barely detectable after 24 hr of ALA treatment (96% reduction relative to t(0)).
source: But even short term (4 hr) ALA feeding triggered a drastic loss of GluTR1 (76% reduction relative to t(0)), while the enzyme was barely detectable after 24 hr of ALA treatment (96% reduction relative to t(0), Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: This strong ALA-induced proteolysis was exclusively observed for GluTR1.
source: This strong ALA-induced proteolysis was exclusively observed for GluTR1.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A showing other proteins are not similarly affected.

claim: Chl a and b content were not changed in ALA- and mock-treated leaves during 24 hr darkness compared to t(0).
source: Furthermore, Chl a and b (Chl a + b, Figure 1B) and non-covalently bound (ncb) heme (Figure 1C) content were not changed in ALA- and mock-treated leaves during 24 hr darkness compared to t(0).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Non-covalently bound (ncb) heme content was not changed in ALA- and mock-treated leaves during 24 hr darkness compared to t(0).
source: Furthermore, Chl a and b (Chl a + b, Figure 1B) and non-covalently bound (ncb) heme (Figure 1C) content were not changed in ALA- and mock-treated leaves during 24 hr darkness compared to t(0).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Pchlide levels increased by 10- and 20-fold in control and approximately 100- and 300-fold in ALA-fed leaves after 4 hr and 24 hr of dark treatment, respectively, in comparison to the steady-state levels detected in the light-grown seedlings.
source: In contrast, the Pchlide levels increased by 10- and 20-fold in control and approximately 100- and 300-fold in ALA-fed leaves after 4 hr and 24 hr of dark treatment, respectively, in comparison to the steady-state levels detected in the light-grown seedlings (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Levels of HEMA1 mRNAs were decreased by at least 60% and up to 95% after 4 hr and 24 hr of dark incubation, respectively, irrespective of ALA supplementation.
source: Irrespective of ALA supplementation, levels of HEMA1 (encoding GluTR1), CHL27, GSA1 (encoding GSAT) and FC2 mRNAs were decreased by at least 60% and up to 95% after 4 hr and 24 hr of dark incubation, respectively (Figure 1E,H,G,J).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The HEMA2 transcript content remained high during dark incubation and was slightly induced by 24 hr of ALA feeding.
source: The HEMA2 transcript content remained high during dark incubation and was slightly induced by 24 hr of ALA feeding (Figure 1F), while FC1 mRNA content increased steadily upon incubation of leaves with ALA (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: FC1 mRNA content increased steadily upon incubation of leaves with ALA.
source: The HEMA2 transcript content remained high during dark incubation and was slightly induced by 24 hr of ALA feeding (Figure 1F), while FC1 mRNA content increased steadily upon incubation of leaves with ALA (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Amounts of GluTR2 and FC1 correlated with the corresponding mRNA levels detected throughout the 24 hr treatment.
source: Amounts of GluTR2 and FC1 correlated with the corresponding mRNA levels detected throughout the 24 hr treatment (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by comparing western blot data in Figure 1A with qRT-PCR data in Figures 1F and 1I.

claim: HEMA1 transcript levels were reduced during dark incubation regardless of the ALA supply.
source: However, HEMA1 transcript levels were reduced during dark incubation regardless of the ALA supply, indicating that excess ALA had no specific effect on the expression of HEMA1 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Excess ALA had no specific effect on the expression of HEMA1.
source: However, HEMA1 transcript levels were reduced during dark incubation regardless of the ALA supply, indicating that excess ALA had no specific effect on the expression of HEMA1 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that HEMA1 transcript levels decreased similarly with and without ALA treatment.

claim: The decreased GluTR1 content observed upon ALA feeding is not a consequence of altered HEMA1 transcription, but is instead attributable to post-translational destabilization of the protein.
source: In summary, it can be concluded that the decreased GluTR1 content observed upon ALA feeding is not a consequence of altered HEMA1 transcription, but is instead attributable to post-translational destabilization of the protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that HEMA1 transcript levels decreased similarly with and without ALA treatment, while GluTR1 protein levels decreased more with ALA treatment.

claim: The GluTR1 content was reduced by 74% in ALA-fed WT leaves compared to the control conditions without ALA after 4 hr.
source: While the GluTR1 content was reduced by 74% in ALA-fed WT leaves compared to the control conditions without ALA, the ALA-incubated clp leaves retained 50% of the starting level of GluTR1 after 4 hr (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The ALA-incubated clp leaves retained 50% of the starting level of GluTR1 after 4 hr.
source: While the GluTR1 content was reduced by 74% in ALA-fed WT leaves compared to the control conditions without ALA, the ALA-incubated clp leaves retained 50% of the starting level of GluTR1 after 4 hr (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Both clpc1-1 and clpr2-1 mutants accumulated WT-like amounts of Pchlide and ncb heme.
source: Both mutants accumulated WT-like amounts of Pchlide and ncb heme, indicating that lower Clp activity does not interfere with ALA uptake or metabolic conversion during the incubation period (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: Lower Clp activity does not interfere with ALA uptake or metabolic conversion during the incubation period.
source: Both mutants accumulated WT-like amounts of Pchlide and ncb heme, indicating that lower Clp activity does not interfere with ALA uptake or metabolic conversion during the incubation period (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that clp mutants accumulated similar amounts of Pchlide and ncb heme as WT.

claim: GluTR1 was almost undetectable in ALA-fed WT leaves after 24 hr.
source: While GluTR1 was almost undetectable in ALA-fed WT leaves after 24 hr, ALA-treated clpc1-1 and clpr2-1 leaves still contained 22–25% of the GluTR1 content detected in untreated samples (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ALA-treated clpc1-1 and clpr2-1 leaves still contained 22–25% of the GluTR1 content detected in untreated samples after 24 hr.
source: While GluTR1 was almost undetectable in ALA-fed WT leaves after 24 hr, ALA-treated clpc1-1 and clpr2-1 leaves still contained 22–25% of the GluTR1 content detected in untreated samples (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The altered Clp activity is correlated with delayed ALA-induced degradation of GluTR1.
source: Thus, the altered Clp activity is correlated with delayed ALA-induced degradation of GluTR1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that clp mutants retain more GluTR1 after ALA treatment than WT.

claim: Diminished Clp protease activity is accompanied by more considerable GluTR1 accumulation under otherwise standard conditions.
source: Additionally, diminished Clp protease activity is accompanied by more considerable GluTR1 accumulation under otherwise standard conditions (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The lack of GBP in the gbp-2 mutant is associated with a 40% reduction in GluTR1 content compared to the WT sample after 24 hr of dark incubation.
source: In agreement with previous results (Apitz et al., 2016), the lack of GBP in the gbp-2 mutant is associated with a 40% reduction in GluTR1 content compared to the WT sample after 24 hr of dark incubation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B and cited previous results.

claim: The 24 hr ALA treatment provoked severe degradation of GluTR1 in WT, and essentially complete loss of the protein in gbp-2 leaves.
source: The 24 hr ALA treatment provoked severe degradation of GluTR1 in WT, and essentially complete loss of the protein in gbp-2 leaves (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both hema1/HEMA1 and hema1/HEMA1(ΔRED) transgenic lines contained similar amounts of GluTR1 to the WT control after 24 hr of incubation in ALA-free buffer.
source: Both transgenic lines contained similar amounts of GluTR1 to the WT control after 24 hr of incubation in ALA-free buffer (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Truncated GluTR1 was not degraded in the hema1/HEMA1(ΔRED) line upon ALA feeding, in contrast to WT and hema1/HEMA1 leaves.
source: Strikingly, however, and in contrast to WT and hema1/HEMA1 leaves, truncated GluTR1 was not degraded in the hema1/HEMA1(ΔRED) line upon ALA feeding (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The amounts of Pchlide and ncb heme detectable after 4 hr of incubation were comparable across all genotypes (WT, gbp-2, hema1/HEMA1, hema1/HEMA1(ΔRED)).
source: The amounts of Pchlide and ncb heme detectable after 4 hr of incubation were comparable across all genotypes (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 3C and 3D (note: text refers to Figure 4C,D but this appears to be an error, should be Figure 3C,D based on context).

claim: Both ACI and DP prevented the ALA-induced degradation of GluTR1 in the PA cultures.
source: Intriguingly, however, both ACI and DP prevented the ALA-induced degradation of GluTR1 in the PA cultures (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: After 4 hr of dark incubation, GluTR1 content was diminished in gun5-2 leaves in the absence of ALA, and even more strongly in the presence of ALA.
source: After 4 hr of dark incubation, GluTR1 content was diminished in gun5-2 leaves in the absence of ALA, and even more strongly in the presence of ALA (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Proteolysis led to almost undetectable levels of GluTR1 in gun5-2 leaves after 24 hr of dark incubation (±ALA).
source: Proteolysis led to almost undetectable levels of GluTR1 in gun5-2 leaves after 24 hr of dark incubation (±ALA), pointing to the heme branch as the source of the degradation signal of GluTR1.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The heme branch is the source of the degradation signal of GluTR1.
source: Proteolysis led to almost undetectable levels of GluTR1 in gun5-2 leaves after 24 hr of dark incubation (±ALA), pointing to the heme branch as the source of the degradation signal of GluTR1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that gun5-2 mutant (which cannot synthesize Mg-branch metabolites) still shows GluTR1 degradation.

claim: Feeding with hemin, but none of other tested tetrapyrroles triggered GluTR1 instability in isolated Arabidopsis chloroplasts.
source: This suggestion was supported by the finding that feeding with hemin, but none of other tested tetrapyrroles triggered GluTR1 instability in isolated Arabidopsis chloroplasts (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: fc2-2 accumulated more GluTR1 relative to WT levels at t(0) under standard growth conditions.
source: Like the clp mutants, fc2-2 accumulated more GluTR1 relative to WT levels at t(0)) under standard growth conditions (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: While 4 hr of ALA-feeding induced GluTR1 proteolysis in WT, the starting content of GluTR1 remained stable in fc2-2.
source: While 4 hr of ALA-feeding induced GluTR1 proteolysis in WT, the starting content of GluTR1 remained stable in fc2-2 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: GluTR1 proteolysis was clearly altered in fc2-2 relative to t(0) after 4 hr and 24 hr ± ALA, in contrast to WT.
source: In contrast to WT, GluTR1 proteolysis was clearly altered in fc2-2 relative to t(0) after 4 hr and 24 hr ± ALA (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: GluTR1 levels in fc2-2 leaves were lower after 24 hr of ALA treatment compared to t(0).
source: However, it is worth mentioning that GluTR1 levels in fc2-2 leaves were lower after 24 hr of ALA treatment compared to t(0), which was not due to diminished Clp content (Figure 5B) nor of lower HEMA1 expression (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The lower GluTR1 levels in fc2-2 leaves after 24 hr of ALA treatment was not due to diminished Clp content.
source: However, it is worth mentioning that GluTR1 levels in fc2-2 leaves were lower after 24 hr of ALA treatment compared to t(0), which was not due to diminished Clp content (Figure 5B) nor of lower HEMA1 expression (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The lower GluTR1 levels in fc2-2 leaves after 24 hr of ALA treatment was not due to lower HEMA1 expression.
source: However, it is worth mentioning that GluTR1 levels in fc2-2 leaves were lower after 24 hr of ALA treatment compared to t(0), which was not due to diminished Clp content (Figure 5B) nor of lower HEMA1 expression (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Overaccumulation of FC1 was observed in detached fc2-2 leaves.
source: However, overaccumulation of FC1 was observed in detached fc2-2 leaves (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The ALA-induced accumulation of ProtoIX and Pchlide was similar in dark-incubated WT and fc2-2 leaves.
source: The ALA-induced accumulation of ProtoIX (Figure 5E) and Pchlide (Figure 5F) was similar in dark-incubated WT and fc2-2 leaves.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 5E and 5F.

claim: fc2-2 accumulated ProtoIX during light exposure and Pchlide in darkness compared to WT without ALA.
source: In comparison to WT without ALA, fc2-2 accumulated ProtoIX during light exposure and Pchlide in darkness (Figure 5E and F) leading to a significant decrease of ncb heme at t(0), but no further decline during dark incubation (both with -ALA and +ALA) (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 5E and 5F.

claim: fc2-2 showed a significant decrease of ncb heme at t(0), but no further decline during dark incubation (both with -ALA and +ALA).
source: In comparison to WT without ALA, fc2-2 accumulated ProtoIX during light exposure and Pchlide in darkness (Figure 5E and F) leading to a significant decrease of ncb heme at t(0), but no further decline during dark incubation (both with -ALA and +ALA) (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Dark incubation of WT leaves in ALA-free buffer did not modify the level of intracellular free heme.
source: While dark incubation of WT leaves in ALA-free buffer did not modify the level of intracellular free heme, supplementation with ALA significantly increased the content of free heme in the WT after 4 hr and 24 hr, respectively (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Supplementation with ALA significantly increased the content of free heme in the WT after 4 hr and 24 hr.
source: While dark incubation of WT leaves in ALA-free buffer did not modify the level of intracellular free heme, supplementation with ALA significantly increased the content of free heme in the WT after 4 hr and 24 hr, respectively (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The overall free heme content was significantly reduced in the fc2-2 leaves.
source: In contrast, the overall free heme content was significantly reduced in the fc2-2 leaves, and FC2 deficiency prevented accumulation of free heme upon ALA feeding (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: FC2 deficiency prevented accumulation of free heme upon ALA feeding.
source: In contrast, the overall free heme content was significantly reduced in the fc2-2 leaves, and FC2 deficiency prevented accumulation of free heme upon ALA feeding (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: An FC1 knockdown mutant showed WT-like GluTR1 content upon ALA supplementation in darkness.
source: For comparison, an FC1 knockdown mutant (FC1 knockout is embryo-lethal) showed WT-like GluTR1 content upon ALA supplementation in darkness (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Genetic impairment of heme biosynthesis caused by the lack of plastid-localized FC2 compromises ALA-induced GluTR1 degradation.
source: In summary, genetic impairment of heme biosynthesis caused by the lack of plastid-localized FC2 compromises ALA-induced GluTR1 degradation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that fc2-2 mutant retains more GluTR1 after ALA treatment than WT.

claim: Both the GST- and HIS-tagged GBP proteins were able to bind to HA, but not to unmodified agarose.
source: Both the GST- and HIS-tagged GBP proteins were able to bind to HA, but not to unmodified agarose (Figure 6A), while none of the tagged GluTR1 variants bound to HA (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: None of the tagged GluTR1 variants bound to HA.
source: Both the GST- and HIS-tagged GBP proteins were able to bind to HA, but not to unmodified agarose (Figure 6A), while none of the tagged GluTR1 variants bound to HA (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: GBP binds specifically to the HA.
source: These results confirm that GBP binds specifically to the HA.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that GBP binds to HA but not to unmodified agarose.

claim: GST-GBP binds to 6xHIS-GluTR1 in the absence of heme.
source: Analysis of in vitro pull-down assays with recombinant 6xHIS-GluTR and GST-GBP in the absence (Figure 7A) or presence of hemin (Figure 7B) revealed GST-GBP binding to 6xHIS-GluTR1 in the absence of heme, while added hemin abolished this interaction (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Added hemin abolished the interaction between GST-GBP and 6xHIS-GluTR1.
source: Analysis of in vitro pull-down assays with recombinant 6xHIS-GluTR and GST-GBP in the absence (Figure 7A) or presence of hemin (Figure 7B) revealed GST-GBP binding to 6xHIS-GluTR1 in the absence of heme, while added hemin abolished this interaction (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: When GluTR1 was titrated against labeled GBP, a Kd value of 65 nM was calculated.
source: When GluTR1 was titrated against labeled GBP (Figure 7C), a Kd value of 65 nM was calculated.
evidence: This is supported by MST data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The Kd value for the GBP-GluTR1-FLUO interaction was 113 nM.
source: Likewise, the Kd value for the GBP-GluTR1-FLUO interaction was 113 nM (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by MST data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Heat inactivation of GluTR1 abolished the interaction with GBP-FLUO.
source: Heat inactivation of GluTR1 abolished the interaction with GBP-FLUO (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by MST data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Addition of 1 µM hemin markedly decreased the affinity between GBP and GluTR1 by 7- to 14-fold.
source: Finally, addition of 1 µM hemin markedly decreased the affinity between the two proteins by 7- to 14-fold (GBP-FLUO: 931 nM / GluTR1-FLUO: 806 nM) (Figure 7C/D).
evidence: This is supported by MST data shown in Figures 7C and 7D.

claim: GluTR1 is a well-established substrate for the Clp protease in plants and bacteria.
source: GluTR1 is a well-established substrate for the Clp protease in plants (Apitz et al., 2016; Nishimura et al., 2015) and bacteria (Wang et al., 1999a), but the factors and signals that regulate the stability of GluTR have been elusive.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: GluTR1 is more stable in the functional knockdown mutants clpc1-1 and clpr2-1 than it is in WT in the presence of excess ALA.
source: In the presence of excess ALA, GluTR1 is more stable in the functional knockdown mutants clpc1-1 and clpr2-1 (Kim et al., 2009; Nishimura and van Wijk, 2015) than it is in WT (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The GluTR1 N-terminal region, including the RED, is recognized by the corresponding Clp subunits.
source: The GluTR1 N-terminal region, including the RED, is recognized by the corresponding Clp subunits (Apitz et al., 2016; Nishimura et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Deletion of the RED renders GluTR1 insensitive to ALA-induced Clp degradation in darkness and prevents proteolysis of ΔRED-GluTR.
source: Consequently, deletion of the RED renders GluTR1 insensitive to ALA-induced Clp degradation in darkness and prevents proteolysis of ΔRED-GluTR (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Knockout of GBP resulted in faster breakdown of GluTR than that seen in WT.
source: In contrast, knockout of GBP (which otherwise counteracts proteolysis) resulted in faster breakdown of GluTR than that seen in WT (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The rapid degradation of GluTR1 in leaves supplemented with ALA is not correlated with declined transcription of HEMA1.
source: The rapid degradation of GluTR1 in leaves supplemented with ALA (Figure 1A), which is not correlated with declined transcription of HEMA1 (Figure 1E), highlights a posttranslational mechanism that specifically controls GluTR1 availability for TBS by excess ALA.
evidence: This is supported by comparing western blot data in Figure 1A with qRT-PCR data in Figure 1E.

claim: A posttranslational mechanism specifically controls GluTR1 availability for TBS by excess ALA.
source: The rapid degradation of GluTR1 in leaves supplemented with ALA (Figure 1A), which is not correlated with declined transcription of HEMA1 (Figure 1E), highlights a posttranslational mechanism that specifically controls GluTR1 availability for TBS by excess ALA.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that GluTR1 protein levels decrease more with ALA treatment while HEMA1 transcript levels decrease similarly with and without ALA treatment.

claim: Accumulation of Pchlide has been reported to induce the FLU-dependent repression of GluTR activity in darkness.
source: Firstly, accumulation of Pchlide has been reported to induce the FLU-dependent repression of GluTR activity in darkness (Meskauskiene et al., 2001; Richter et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: An N-terminally truncated recombinant GluTR1 was shown to be insensitive to heme-dependent feedback regulation.
source: Secondly, heme-dependent feedback regulation of GluTR was suggested in previous studies, and an N-terminally truncated recombinant GluTR1 was shown to be insensitive to it (Terry and Kendrick, 1996; Terry and Kendrick, 1999; Vothknecht et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Inhibition of Pchlide and heme accumulation at the levels of PPOX, FC and oxidative cyclase, respectively, prevents ALA-induced GluTR1 proteolysis in a photoautotrophic cell culture.
source: 1. Inhibition of Pchlide and heme accumulation at the levels of PPOX, FC and oxidative cyclase, respectively, prevents ALA-induced GluTR1 proteolysis in a photoautotrophic cell culture (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Supplementation of purified Arabidopsis chloroplasts with various tetrapyrroles identified heme as the stimulatory factor for GluTR1 degradation.
source: 2. Supplementation of purified Arabidopsis chloroplasts with various tetrapyrroles identified heme as the stimulatory factor for GluTR1 degradation (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The ALA-fed gun5-2 knockout mutant exhibits ALA-induced GluTR1 degradation, revealing that the process is not triggered by metabolites of the Chl-synthesizing branch.
source: 3. The ALA-fed gun5-2 knockout mutant exhibits ALA-induced GluTR1 degradation, revealing that the process is not triggered by metabolites of the Chl-synthesizing branch (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4E and inferred from the fact that gun5-2 cannot synthesize Mg-branch metabolites.

claim: ALA-fed fc2-2 leaves retain GluTR1 in the darkness.
source: 4. The final proof for the feedback regulatory function of heme was obtained when ALA-fed fc2-2 leaves were found to retain GluTR1 in the darkness (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Significantly different contents of 'free' heme were observed in ALA-fed WT and fc2-2 leaves.
source: We also observed significantly different contents of 'free' heme in ALA-fed WT and fc2-2 leaves (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The increased FC1 content only partially compensated for the deficit of FC2 activity and did not lead to adequate heme synthesis in plastids.
source: The increased FC1 content (Figure 5B) only partially compensated for the deficit of FC2 activity and did not lead to adequate heme synthesis in plastids.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that fc2-2 has increased FC1 but still shows reduced free heme levels.

claim: Heme synthesized by FC2 is allocated for GBP-binding, while FC1 provides heme for other cellular compartments.
source: Therefore, it is proposed that heme synthesized by FC2 is allocated for GBP-binding, while FC1 provides heme for other cellular compartments, as it has been proposed previously (Espinas et al., 2016; Scharfenberg et al., 2015).
evidence: This is proposed based on the data and previous studies cited.

claim: Lack of heme synthesis by FC2 correlates with greater stability of GluTR1 during short-term ALA feeding in the darkness.
source: In conclusion, lack of heme synthesis by FC2 correlates with greater stability of GluTR1 during short-term ALA feeding in the darkness.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that fc2-2 mutant retains more GluTR1 after ALA treatment than WT.

claim: The involvement of heme in the regulation of ALA synthesis constitutes one among the many post-translational mechanisms that control GluTR.
source: Thus, the involvement of heme in the regulation of ALA synthesis constitutes one among the many post-translational mechanisms that control GluTR.
evidence: This is inferred from the data presented and the context of other known regulatory mechanisms.

claim: GluTR1 degradation was indeed also observed in fc2-2 after 24 hr of incubation with ALA, but was significantly less pronounced than in the WT.
source: GluTR1 degradation was indeed also observed in fc2-2 after 24 hr of incubation with ALA, but was significantly less pronounced than in the WT (Figure 5B), indicating the existence of an additional proteolysis pathway that is independent of FC2-synthesized heme.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There exists an additional proteolysis pathway that is independent of FC2-synthesized heme.
source: GluTR1 degradation was indeed also observed in fc2-2 after 24 hr of incubation with ALA, but was significantly less pronounced than in the WT (Figure 5B), indicating the existence of an additional proteolysis pathway that is independent of FC2-synthesized heme.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that GluTR1 is still degraded in fc2-2 after 24 hr, albeit less than in WT.

claim: The elevated FC1 content seen in fc2-2 could also contribute to the synthesis of regulatory heme.
source: Alternatively, the elevated FC1 content seen in fc2-2 (Figure 5B) could also contribute to the synthesis of regulatory heme.
evidence: This is proposed as a speculation based on the observation of elevated FC1 in fc2-2.

claim: There is a structural homology between GBP and the bacterial heme oxygenase HugZ.
source: Previous studies revealed a structural homology between GBP and the bacterial heme oxygenase HugZ, which converts heme into biliverdin (Hu et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Co-filtration and isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) have demonstrated binding of heme to GBP.
source: Although the order of domains differs in GBP from that of HugZ and its mode of heme-binding has not been analyzed, co-filtration and isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) have demonstrated binding of heme to GBP (Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: The hemin-agarose-based binding assays unequivocally validate GBP as a heme-binding protein.
source: The hemin-agarose-based binding assays described here unequivocally validate GBP as a heme-binding protein (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The inability of GluTR1 to bind hemin agrees with the absence of bound heme in GluTR1 crystal structures.
source: The inability of GluTR1 to bind hemin in this assay (Figure 6B) agrees with the absence of bound heme in GluTR1 crystal structures (Fang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B and cited crystal structure studies.

claim: Heme-free GBP binds to GluTR1.
source: The regulatory model shown in Figure 8 depicts binding of heme-free GBP to GluTR1.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: GBP can bind either to GluTR or to heme.
source: Thus, we propose that GBP can bind either to GluTR or to heme, and as long as the GBP is bound to GluTR1, the recognition site for Clp subunits near the GluTR N-terminus is masked (Apitz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is proposed based on the experimental data showing mutually exclusive binding.

claim: As long as the GBP is bound to GluTR1, the recognition site for Clp subunits near the GluTR N-terminus is masked.
source: Thus, we propose that GBP can bind either to GluTR or to heme, and as long as the GBP is bound to GluTR1, the recognition site for Clp subunits near the GluTR N-terminus is masked (Apitz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is proposed based on the experimental data and cited previous studies.

claim: Heme functions as the trigger for reduced ALA synthesis by binding to GBP.
source: Hence, an effector molecule is needed to regulate the conditional stability of GluTR1. We propose that heme functions as the trigger for reduced ALA synthesis by binding to GBP.
evidence: This is proposed based on the experimental data.

claim: Heme-dependent attenuation of the GluTR1-GBP interaction supports the assumption that heme functions as the trigger for reduced ALA synthesis.
source: This assumption is supported by heme-dependent attenuation of the GluTR1-GBP interaction (Figure 7A,B) and the strongly decreased affinity of heme-bound GBP for GluTR1 demonstrated by MST measurements (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is supported by pull-down and MST data shown in Figures 7A, 7B, 7C, and 7D.

claim: The negative impact of heme on the GBP-GluTR interaction is in agreement with decreased stimulation of GluTR activity by GBP in the presence of heme.
source: The negative impact of heme on the GBP-GluTR interaction is in agreement with decreased stimulation of GluTR activity by GBP in the presence of heme (Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: GBP binds to both Arabidopsis GluTR isoforms, encoded by HEMA1 and HEMA2.
source: GBP binds to both Arabidopsis GluTR isoforms, encoded by HEMA1 and HEMA2 (Czarnecki et al., 2011), suggesting that GluTR2 is also regulated by heme-bound GBP.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: GluTR2 is also regulated by heme-bound GBP.
source: GBP binds to both Arabidopsis GluTR isoforms, encoded by HEMA1 and HEMA2 (Czarnecki et al., 2011), suggesting that GluTR2 is also regulated by heme-bound GBP.
evidence: This is suggested based on the observation that GBP binds to both GluTR isoforms.

claim: GluTR2 is not degraded during ALA feeding.
source: However, GluTR2 is not degraded during ALA feeding in our study (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The N-terminal region of GluTR2 lacks four amino acids relative to the RED of GluTR1.
source: A sequence alignment of Arabidopsis GluTR1 and GluTR2 reveals that the N-terminal region of GluTR2 lacks four amino acids relative to the RED of GluTR1 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Binding to FLU likely prevents Clp-dependent degradation of GluTR.
source: Although binding to FLU likely prevents Clp-dependent degradation of GluTR (Hou et al., 2019), we propose that FLU and heme act in concert to control ALA synthesis in plants (Goslings et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: FLU and heme act in concert to control ALA synthesis in plants.
source: Although binding to FLU likely prevents Clp-dependent degradation of GluTR (Hou et al., 2019), we propose that FLU and heme act in concert to control ALA synthesis in plants (Goslings et al., 2004).
evidence: This is proposed based on the data and cited previous studies.

claim: Heterotrophic tissues, which do not synthesize Chl (e.g. roots), do not utilize the FLU-POR-Pchlide inactivation complex to control ALA synthesis.
source: In contrast, heterotrophic tissues, which do not synthesize Chl (e.g. roots), do not utilize the FLU-POR-Pchlide inactivation complex to control ALA synthesis (Kauss et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: In heterotrophic tissues, heme presumably serves as the sole signal that triggers the adjustment of GluTR amounts and ALA synthesis rates.
source: Here, heme presumably serves as the sole signal that triggers the adjustment of GluTR amounts and ALA synthesis rates.
evidence: This is proposed based on the data and the context of heterotrophic tissues lacking FLU-POR-Pchlide complex.

claim: The heme status controls GluTR amounts and activity in bacteria.
source: Although the precise mechanism is still unknown, the heme status also controls GluTR amounts and activity in bacteria (Wang et al., 1999a; Wang et al., 1999b; de Armas-Ricard et al., 2011), implying that the GluTR proteolysis mechanism evolved early in evolutionary history.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: The GluTR proteolysis mechanism evolved early in evolutionary history.
source: Although the precise mechanism is still unknown, the heme status also controls GluTR amounts and activity in bacteria (Wang et al., 1999a; Wang et al., 1999b; de Armas-Ricard et al., 2011), implying that the GluTR proteolysis mechanism evolved early in evolutionary history.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that heme controls GluTR in both plants and bacteria.

claim: Homologs of GBP and the RED of GluTR1 are only found in land plants.
source: Phylogenetic analysis reveals, however, that homologs of GBP and the RED of GluTR1 are only found in land plants (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: GBP and RED have coevolved for the regulation of GluTR stability by heme.
source: In light of the fact that angiosperms lacking dark-dependent POR (DPOR) need to control ALA synthesis during light-dark cycles tightly, it is reasonable to assume that GBP and RED have coevolved for the regulation of GluTR stability by heme.
evidence: This is proposed based on the phylogenetic data and the context of angiosperm biology.

claim: Regulation of Chl synthesis by modulated GluTR stability was proposed to play a minor role in Chlamydomonas.
source: In this line, regulation of Chl synthesis by modulated GluTR stability was proposed to play a minor role in Chlamydomonas (Nogaj et al., 2005) suggesting a posttranslationally adjusted GluTR activity.
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: A flu phenotype has been noted in the fc2-2 mutant, that is, light-dependent necrosis owing to the overaccumulation of TBS intermediates during darkness.
source: A flu phenotype has been noted in the fc2-2 mutant, that is, light-dependent necrosis owing to the overaccumulation of TBS intermediates during darkness (Scharfenberg et al., 2015; Woodson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: The flu phenotype in fc2-2 can be explained by the diminished synthesis of heme functioning as the stimulus for GluTR1 degradation.
source: This observation can now be explained by the diminished synthesis of heme functioning as the stimulus for GluTR1 degradation (Figure 5).
evidence: This is inferred from the data presented in Figure 5.

claim: The aurea (au) and yellow-green 2 (yg-2) mutants of tomato show a pale-green phenotype which is related to enhanced inhibition of ALA synthesis.
source: Furthermore, the aurea (au) and yellow-green 2 (yg-2) mutants of tomato, which are defective in the phytochromobilin synthase and heme oxygenase (HO/HY1) respectively, show a pale-green phenotype which is related to enhanced inhibition of ALA synthesis (Terry and Kendrick, 1996; Terry and Kendrick, 1999).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Accumulation of heme owing to impaired heme conversion to phytochromobilin in au and yg-2 mutants was assumed to inhibit GluTR activity.
source: Accumulation of heme owing to impaired heme conversion to phytochromobilin in these mutants was assumed to inhibit GluTR activity. This was also observed in assays with a recombinant plant GluTR (Vothknecht et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Introduction of a HO1 mutation into a flu mutant background rescued the flu phenotype by alleviating Pchlide accumulation.
source: Additionally, introduction of a HO1 mutation into a flu mutant background rescued the flu phenotype by alleviating Pchlide accumulation (Goslings et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Early work on ALA synthesis in cucumber plastids and etiolated bean seedlings treated with dipyridyl and heme, respectively, revealed heme-dependent inhibition of ALA synthesis.
source: Furthermore, early work on ALA synthesis in cucumber plastids and etiolated bean seedlings treated with dipyridyl and heme, respectively, revealed heme-dependent inhibition of ALA synthesis (Chereskin and Castelfranco, 1982; Duggan and Gassman, 1974).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Diminished ALA synthesis in au, yg-2 and flu/hy1 mutants results from GluTR breakdown which is due to alterations of heme metabolism and modified levels of regulatory heme.
source: Based on our new findings, it is reasonable to propose that diminishes ALA synthesis in au, yg-2 and flu/hy1 mutants results from GluTR breakdown which is due to alterations of heme metabolism and modified levels of regulatory heme.
evidence: This is proposed based on the new findings presented in this study.
